records.title: feat: Apache AGE graph store replacing recursive CTEs
records.body:
## Context
Deferred Task 5.2 from `docs/planning/backend-db-implementation.xml`.
Depends on: Task 5.1 (Apache AGE Docker image).

## Description
Implement `GraphStore` interface using Apache AGE Cypher queries. Replace the iterative Python graph traversal in `AsyncEdgeRepository.get_neighbors()` with native Cypher queries for complex traversals.

The current implementation uses Python-side BFS over edge table queries. AGE would enable single-query traversals like:
```cypher
MATCH (a)-[r*1..3]->(b) WHERE a.entity_id = $id RETURN b, r
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AGE-backed GraphStore passes existing edge repository tests
- [ ] Cypher queries for 1-hop, 2-hop, and 3-hop traversals
- [ ] Performance comparison: recursive CTE vs AGE Cypher
- [ ] Fallback to CTE implementation when AGE unavailable

records.title: P2-02: Project CRUD API -- Tree View, Search, Assignment Management
records.body:
## Goal

Build the Project CRUD API: list (with tree view), create (top-level or sub-project), update, archive/unarchive, search, and project assignment management. This is the backend for all project management operations.

## Background & Context

Projects must be manageable via API for web, mobile, and MCP clients. The tree structure requires special serialization (nested children). Project assignment manages which employees are linked to which projects.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `GET /api/projects/` -- list root projects (flat, with child_count)
- [ ] `GET /api/projects/?tree=true` -- full tree (nested JSON)
- [ ] `GET /api/projects/?search=term` -- search by name or code
- [ ] `GET /api/projects/?active_only=true` -- filter active projects
- [ ] `GET /api/projects/{id}/` -- single project with immediate children
- [ ] `POST /api/projects/` -- create project (parent_id optional for sub-project)
- [ ] `PATCH /api/projects/{id}/` -- update name, description, billable, client_name, budget_hours
- [ ] `POST /api/projects/{id}/archive/` -- archive project + descendants
- [ ] `POST /api/projects/{id}/unarchive/` -- reactivate project only
- [ ] `POST /api/projects/{id}/assign/` -- assign employee to project
- [ ] `DELETE /api/projects/{id}/assignments/{assignment_id}/` -- remove assignment
- [ ] `GET /api/projects/{id}/assignments/` -- list assigned employees
- [ ] RBAC: manager+ for create/update/archive, employee+ for read
- [ ] Audit log entries for all mutations

## Architecture Notes

- ProjectService encapsulates all business logic
- Tree serializer: `ProjectTreeSerializer` with recursive `children` field
- Search uses `icontains` on name and `istartswith` on code
- ProjectService injected with AuditService and RBACService

## Files to Create

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `backend/projects/views.py` | `ProjectViewSet`, `ProjectAssignmentViewSet` |
| `backend/projects/serializers.py` | `ProjectSerializer`, `ProjectTreeSerializer`, `ProjectAssignmentSerializer` |
| `backend/projects/services/project_service.py` | `ProjectService` |
| `backend/projects/urls.py` | URL routing |
| `backend/config/urls.py` | Include projects URLs |

## Implementation Notes

```python
class ProjectService:
    def __init__(self, audit_service: AuditService, rbac_service: RBACService):
        self._audit = audit_service
        self._rbac = rbac_service

    def create_project(self, actor: User, data: dict) -> Project:
        parent_id = data.pop("parent_id", None)
        code = self._generate_next_code()
        if parent_id:
            parent = Project.objects.get(id=parent_id)
            project = parent.add_child(code=code, **data, created_by=actor)
        else:
            project = Project.add_root(code=code, **data, created_by=actor)
        self._audit.log_action(actor, "CREATE", "Project", project.pk, new_values=data)
        return project

    def archive_project(self, actor: User, project: Project) -> None:
        descendants = project.get_descendants()
        project.is_active = False
        project.save(update_fields=["is_active", "updated_at"])
        descendants.update(is_active=False)
        self._audit.log_action(actor, "UPDATE", "Project", project.pk,
                               old_values={"is_active": True}, new_values={"is_active": False})
```

## Test Requirements

- [ ] Create root project returns auto-generated code
- [ ] Create sub-project as child
- [ ] Tree endpoint returns nested JSON structure
- [ ] Search by name and code works
- [ ] Archive cascades to descendants
- [ ] Unarchive affects only target project
- [ ] Assignment creates employee-project link
- [ ] Remove assignment works
- [ ] RBAC: employee cannot create project, manager can
- [ ] Audit entries created for all mutations

## Definition of Done

`make test` passes. All CRUD endpoints functional. Tree view returns correct nesting.

## Dependencies

- **Depends-On:** #P2-01 (Project model), #38 (P1-11: AuditService), #33 (P1-06: RBAC)

records.title: Kleene `+`/`*` semantics
records.body:
# Language-level Kleene `+` / `*` via an ENFORCE fixpoint — semantics, machine-checked proofs, and a shrinking-safe plan

## What this issue is

A design proposal (with machine-checked semantics) to make the Kleene operators `+` and `*` a *first-class, maintained* part of the language by **desugaring** them into a fresh relation plus an `ENFORCE` fixpoint, rather than treating them as a special SQL construct. The goal is to close the gap that the docs still record — *"the Kleene operators are not fully implemented yet"* (`docs/reference-material/terms.md`) — including the case that has blocked a full solution so far: **maintenance under deletion (shrinking)**.

This issue documents the reasoning with proofs.

## Current state

The operators are *partially* there, and several issues already touch this. My reading:

- **#1488 "Transitive Closure"** (closed as dup of #137) — the original "implement it". States the crux precisely: the known work-arounds only work while the closure **grows monotonically**; a proper solution must also let it **shrink**. Proposes a graduate assignment; refs Dong, Libkin, Su & Wong, *Maintaining Transitive Closure of Graphs in SQL* (1999).
- **#1642 "Add runtime regression tests for `*`/`+` code generation"** (open) — confirms `+`/`*` **parse and type-check**, and the SQL generator already emits a `WITH RECURSIVE TransitiveClosure` CTE for read/check queries. Open gaps: no runtime regression tests, and `ENFORCE rel := r+` trips the **oscillation detector** (a false positive; the bound `r+` is relation-free in `rel`, so it converges in one round).
- **#1635 "Four Kleene laws in tceDerivRules are unsound"** (open) — `r* = r;r*`, `r+ = r;r+` etc. are unsound in the set-of-pairs model; the sound unfoldings are `r* = I ∪ r;r*`, `r+ = r ∪ r;r+`. Found via an Isabelle/HOL encoding of Ampersand's RA.
- **#1526** (closed) — `r+`/`r*` in an `INTERFACE` gave a 503 at runtime on RAP.
- **#137** — the original "SQL cannot create closures".

This issue attempts to consolidate the design behind them.
- #1642 keeps its scope (runtime regression tests); this issue supplies the semantics those tests should pin down, and a principled answer to its oscillation-detector question (certify `ENFORCE >: <fixpoint>` as convergent — see comment 3).
- #1635 keeps its scope (fix the four laws in `NormalForms.hs`); this issue supplies the **sound** laws with machine-checked proofs (comment 2).
- #1488 / #137 were the "please implement" issues; the design here — desugaring + a shrinking strategy — is the missing piece they asked for.

## The request

1. Adopt a **desugaring** of `r+` / `r*` in the front-end: a fresh relation maintained by a monotone `ENFORCE` fixpoint, so the operators become ordinary relations everywhere (including interface terms, which #1488 noted cannot avoid them).
2. Pick a **maintenance strategy that also handles shrinking** (comment 3), defaulting to recompute, with an incremental fast path when the base relation is a forest.
3. Base the whole thing on the machine-checked semantics in comment 2.

Comments below: **(2)** the maths + Isabelle/HOL proofs, **(3)** the preprocessor proposal + correctness, **(4)** efficiency (Warshall front-end; eliminating `*`/`+` from rules via a recursive rule).

Platform drift is a large inline JS implementation checking shallow structure, duplicating policy, mishandling infra repos; the standing checks this plan needs (tree parity, tag ancestry, SHA pins, matrix drift, pin currency, README sections, release traceability) don't exist as machinery.

## Root cause

Fleet policy and implementation evolved in separate repositories without one enforced source of truth or evidence gate. Platform drift is a large inline JS implementation checking shallow structure, duplicating policy, mishandling infra repos; the standing checks this plan needs (tree parity, tag ancestry, SHA pins, matrix drift, pin currency, README sections, release traceability) don't exist as machinery.

## Desired outcome

SHA-pin a released CLI in the scheduled workflow; atya doctor --fleet with manifest-driven archetypes emitting machine-readable results into the existing read-only issue flow; checks: master==development trees, newest-tag ancestry, workflow SHA == fleet pin, csproj refs == manifest edges, global.json == fleet-current, README mandatory sections, tag/Release/NuGet traceability; fixture-tested exceptions; no fleet mutation.

## Affected scope

Primary owner: **Atya.Roadmap**. Audit-affected repositories or coordination scopes: Atya.Roadmap, Cli, platform. Only the cited findings and their direct acceptance evidence are added; unaffected architecture remains unchanged.

## In-scope work

platform drift workflow; CLI. SHA-pin a released CLI in the scheduled workflow; atya doctor --fleet with manifest-driven archetypes emitting machine-readable results into the existing read-only issue flow; checks: master==development trees, newest-tag ancestry, workflow SHA == fleet pin, csproj refs == manifest edges, global.json == fleet-current, README mandatory sections, tag/Release/NuGet traceability; fixture-tested exceptions; no fleet mutation.

## Out-of-scope work

Unrelated repositories or public APIs, speculative package creation, and destructive cleanup not explicitly named by this task.

## Hard dependencies

- ATYA-038
- ATYA-019
- ATYA-001
- ATYA-124

## Advisory prerequisites

None. Advisory prerequisites are nonblocking and do not affect Ready/Blocked status.

## Related tasks

- ATYA-001
- ATYA-002
- ATYA-003

## Implementation sequence

1. Inspect the cited repository paths, public APIs, workflows, tests, tags, and open work before changing anything.
2. SHA-pin a released CLI in the scheduled workflow
3. atya doctor --fleet with manifest-driven archetypes emitting machine-readable results into the existing read-only issue flow
4. checks: master==development trees, newest-tag ancestry, workflow SHA == fleet pin, csproj refs == manifest edges, global.json == fleet-current, README mandatory sections, tag/Release/NuGet traceability
5. fixture-tested exceptions
6. Record Confirmed, Refuted, or Partial evidence and re-scope dependents without implementing unapproved fixes.
7. Update documentation, migration notes, API/release baselines, and roadmap evidence; run every validation command and attach results.

## Architecture guidance

Keep cross-repository policy and generated inventory in Atya.Roadmap/platform authority; package repositories consume generated artifacts and must not fork policy copies.

## Compatibility and migration

Old drift workflow retired after one overlapping cycle.

## Security and privacy considerations

Apply least privilege, treat repository and payload inputs as hostile, redact secrets and internal diagnostics by default, bound untrusted input size/cardinality, and add negative/adversarial tests for the affected trust boundary.

## Testing strategy

Translate every acceptance criterion into an automated regression, conformance, fixture, or scenario test where possible. Include negative and boundary cases; preserve existing tests. Source-specific validation: Seeded-drift canary..

## Documentation work

Update Atya.Roadmap README/architecture material, migration or release notes, and Atya.Roadmap evidence. Link any ADR and identify the last compatible behavior/version.

## Measurable acceptance criteria

- All findings of both source reviews would have been caught by the check set (walk the list and prove coverage); scheduled run green on the repaired fleet, red on seeded drift.

## Definition of done

- All acceptance criteria pass with durable evid

records.title: Add recursive change reconstruction, review, and stacked-delivery workflow
records.body:
## Goal

Add a Project Space / IDE workflow for **reconstructing a change set from zero trust**: every existing change starts outside the accepted result and must be explicitly looked at and re-added before it survives.

The workflow must work for:

- reviewing an already-implemented feature as if its code had never been read;
- recursively decomposing a large PR / branch into smaller reviewable pieces;
- splitting accepted work into multiple stacked PRs;
- pausing with large parts deliberately deferred and resuming later;
- periodically refactoring / reconstructing an entire codebase from a known-good checkpoint.

The core model is broader than PR review:

```text
Source / Candidate Change Set
          ↓
Recursive Decomposition Tree
          ↓
Explicit Reconstruction Review
          ↓
Reviewed Change Set / Tree
          ↓
Delivery Stack or New Codebase Checkpoint
```

Git branches, stashes, patches, and temporary commits are implementation details around this model.

## Zero-trust reconstruction rule

The key behavior is the opposite of a normal review.

Normal review implicitly trusts the candidate and looks for bad parts.

This workflow starts with **nothing implicitly accepted**:

```text
Candidate changes
      ↓
Unreviewed / Deferred pool
      ↓ explicit inspection
Accepted | Rejected | Deferred
```

A change only enters the reviewed result after the reviewer deliberately re-adds it.

This prevents an accidental earlier "approve all" state from bypassing the review. The workflow should make it impossible to claim complete reconstruction while unseen/deferred pieces remain.

## Recursive divide-and-conquer decomposition

A large change set can be split recursively until each piece is small enough to understand.

Example:

```text
Δ Feature
├── Backend
│   ├── Auth
│   │   ├── A1
│   │   └── A2
│   └── Persistence
│       ├── P1
│       └── P2
└── Frontend
    ├── F1
    └── F2
```

A split must be lossless. At every decomposition node:

```text
parent change set == composition of all child change sets
```

The complete leaf set must still reconstruct the original candidate:

```text
replay(all leaf pieces) == original feature/candidate tree
```

Splitting may be implemented with stashes, patches, temporary branches/commits, or another internal representation, but Project Space should expose the conceptual decomposition tree rather than force users to manage raw Git primitives manually.

Pieces may be decomposed by directory, file, hunk, symbol, semantic responsibility, dependency boundary, or another supported strategy.

## Review states

Every piece should have an explicit state:

- **Accepted** — deliberately reviewed and included in the reconstructed result;
- **Rejected** — deliberately reviewed and excluded;
- **Deferred** — intentionally not reviewed yet and available for later continuation.

The accounting invariant is:

```text
Accepted + Rejected + Deferred == original candidate change set
```

No piece may disappear silently.

Review completeness requires:

```text
Deferred == ∅
```

when the user wants to claim that the whole candidate has been reviewed.

A user may deliberately stop earlier and persist the reconstruction session with some parts deferred.

## Feature-branch review workflow

Given a feature branch, create a temporary local review workspace/branch from the known base/checkpoint.

Conceptually:

```bash
git switch <base>
git switch -c review/<feature>
git merge --squash <feature>
git reset --mixed
```

This places the complete feature change set into an unstaged working state.

The reviewer then explicitly reconstructs the desired result by accepting selected files/hunks/pieces and committing the reviewed tree.

The original feature branch remains unchanged during reconstruction.

The temporary review branch is local/disposable once the reviewed result and delivery output have been generated and verified.

## Final cleanup diff

After reconstruction:

```text
Original Feature Tree
        ↓
Reviewed Tree
```

The diff between them is the **cleanup diff**: everything that must be removed or changed on the original feature branch to make it equal the reviewed result.

This gives a strong post-condition:

```text
diff(feature, reviewed) == deliberately rejected/reworked cleanup
```

Applying that cleanup to the feature branch should produce the exact reviewed tree.

## Split accepted changes into stacked PRs

The reviewed change set can then be partitioned into multiple ordered delivery layers.

Example:

```text
base
 └─ pr-1        A
     └─ pr-2    A + B
         └─ pr-3 A + B + C

reviewed tree = A + B + C
```

For each new layer, derive the remaining candidate work from:

```text
diff(current stack head, reviewed tree)
```

The reviewer can select only the pieces that belong in that layer and defer the rest to later layers.

Final delivery completeness requires:

```text
tree(topmost stack branch) == tree(reviewed tree)
```

This proves that every accepted change was ass

records.title: PERF-02 — Core operation benchmarks
records.body:
## Context

The milestone asks that "Core operations have measured performance characteristics" and that "No critical operation exhibits unacceptable behavior at the intended MVP scale." The value is in having numbers at all: without them, "is this slow?" is answered by opinion, and a regression is only noticed when someone complains.

Some coverage exists — `hot_paths_perf_test.go` and `reach_out_trigger_perf_test.go` — but as scattered tests rather than a suite with recorded baselines.

The operations worth measuring are the ones whose cost grows with data, not the ones that happen to be called often:

- contact list with pagination, filters, and sorting
- contact detail, which assembles the full nested `Card` plus projections
- FTS search across `contacts_fts`, `notes_fts`, `activities_fts`
- relationship traversal, especially multi-hop and through dense hubs
- the dashboard and its aggregates
- reach-out and cadence computation over the whole contact set
- duplicate detection, which is inherently pairwise and the most likely quadratic surprise
- contact merge, which repoints every association
- delete cascade, which enumerates every dependent table by hand

## Recommended actions

1. Benchmark each operation at each profile from #468, recording wall-clock time and query count. Query count matters as much as duration: an N+1 that is invisible at 100 contacts is the thing that breaks at 10,000, and it shows up in the count long before it shows up in the clock.
2. Run against a real migrated schema (CLAUDE.md trap #1). Index behavior is the entire subject here, and `AutoMigrate` does not reproduce the hand-written indexes or the FTS triggers.
3. Record baselines as committed data so change is visible over time, rather than printing numbers into a CI log nobody reads. #471 turns these into budgets; this ticket produces the measurements.
4. Look for the shape of the cost, not just its value. Measure each operation at two or more scales and check whether it grows linearly — a quadratic operation that is fast at the typical profile is a future outage, and it is only detectable by comparing across scales.
5. Measure the pathological records specifically, not just the average. The contact with forty phones and a hundred relationships is a real user's real contact.
6. Include the write path, not only reads: create, update, and merge under the concurrency `loadsmoke` already exercises, since write contention on SQLite is a different constraint from read cost.

## How to verify

- Every listed operation has a recorded measurement at every profile.
- Query counts are recorded alongside durations.
- Growth across scales is recorded, and any super-linear operation is flagged as a finding, not just a number.
- Benchmarks run against the real migrated schema.
- Baselines are committed and diffable.
- Hand-verify per CLAUDE.md: introduce an N+1 into one endpoint and confirm the query-count assertion catches it. Restore.

## Notes

Milestone `v0.6.9`. Depends on #468 (fixtures). Feeds #471 (budgets). Related: #470 (data-movement benchmarks), #498 (constrained resources), #263 (Android macrobenchmark — the client-side analogue). Existing: `backend/controllers/hot_paths_perf_test.go`, `backend/services/reach_out_trigger_perf_test.go`, `backend/cmd/loadsmoke`. CLAUDE.md trap #1. Gate: #539.

records.title: Replace recursive SELECTs with SQL recursive CTE in CategoriesService
records.body:
## Priority: HIGH

## Issue Description

Two methods use recursive SELECT patterns that are **extremely slow** for deep category trees:

1. `isDescendant()` - Checks if target is descendant of category
2. `updateChildrenLevels()` - Updates levels of all children recursively

Both perform **N+1 queries** and risk **stack overflow** on large hierarchies.

## Problem: isDescendant()

Current implementation:
```typescript
private static async isDescendant(supabase, targetId, categoryId) {
  const target = await this.getCategoryById(supabase, targetId);
  if (!target) return false;
  if (target.parent_id === categoryId) return true;
  if (!target.parent_id) return false;
  return this.isDescendant(supabase, target.parent_id, categoryId);  // Recursion!
}
```

**Performance**: O(depth) queries for each check.

## Problem: updateChildrenLevels()

Current implementation:
```typescript
private static async updateChildrenLevels(supabase, parentId, parentLevel) {
  const { data: children } = await supabase.select(...).eq("parent_id", parentId);
  
  for (const child of children) {
    await supabase.update({ level: ... }).eq("id", child.id);
    await this.updateChildrenLevels(supabase, child.id, newChildLevel);  // Recursion!
  }
}
```

**Performance**: O(n) queries where n = total descendants.

## Required Fix

Replace with SQL recursive CTEs:

### isDescendant CTE

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION is_descendant(
  p_target_id uuid,
  p_category_id uuid
) RETURNS boolean AS $$
DECLARE
  is_desc boolean;
BEGIN
  WITH RECURSIVE ancestors AS (
    SELECT id, parent_id
    FROM product_categories
    WHERE id = p_target_id
    
    UNION ALL
    
    SELECT c.id, c.parent_id
    FROM product_categories c
    JOIN ancestors a ON c.id = a.parent_id
  )
  SELECT EXISTS(
    SELECT 1 FROM ancestors WHERE id = p_category_id
  ) INTO is_desc;
  
  RETURN is_desc;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
```

### updateChildrenLevels CTE

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION update_children_levels(
  p_parent_id uuid,
  p_parent_level int
) RETURNS void AS $$
BEGIN
  WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT id, parent_id, p_parent_level + 1 as new_level
    FROM product_categories
    WHERE parent_id = p_parent_id
    
    UNION ALL
    
    SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, tree.new_level + 1
    FROM product_categories c
    JOIN tree ON c.parent_id = tree.id
  )
  UPDATE product_categories
  SET level = tree.new_level
  FROM tree
  WHERE product_categories.id = tree.id;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
```

## Benefits

- **Performance**: O(1) query instead of O(n) queries
- **Safety**: No stack overflow risk
- **Atomicity**: Single transaction
- **Scalability**: Works with 1000+ category tree

## Tasks

- [ ] Create migration with RPC functions
- [ ] Replace `isDescendant()` with RPC call

records.title: Complete the segmentation implementation
records.body:
Commit 89509134074bbb0eb75fad8bcc5b45318e35ae9a is a large architectural change. It introduced at least one regression (#645), which is getting fixed. But there are several TODOs/FIXMEs.

Major Incomplete Aspects from the Segmentation Commit

 ### 1. Segment splitting can produce over-sized segments (FIXME)

 ColumnChunkData::split() splits into chunks of 64 values per pass, but doesn't handle the case where a single batch of 64 values still exceeds MAX_SEGMENT_SIZE. The FIXME reads:

 │ "we either need to split recursively, or detect individual values which bring the size above MAX_SEGMENT_SIZE, since this will still sometimes produce segments larger than MAX_SEGMENT_SIZE"

 So for wide rows (e.g., a struct column with many large string children), segments can still exceed the configured cap.

 ### 2. CSR (adjacency-list) node groups lack segmentation (FIXME)

 │ "this needs segmentation. Maybe this should use (or share code with) checkpointOutOfPlace"

 The segmentation was implemented for regular ChunkedNodeGroup columns, but CSR chunked node groups — which store the adjacency lists for relationships — still flush all their data chunks as monolithic blocks without splitting. This is a significant gap since CSR data can be very large.

 ### 3. shouldSplit() computes on-disk size serially (TODO)

 │ "this should use the inMemoryStats to avoid scanning the data, however not all functions update them"

 To decide whether a segment needs splitting, shouldSplit() calls getSizeOnDisk(), which serializes the entire segment to measure its byte size. This is expensive for in-memory data. It should use cached in-memory statistics instead, but those aren't reliably maintained by all code paths.

 ### 4. O(N²) ALP metadata in split (fixed post-commit)

 The initial split() implementation recomputed ALP compression metadata from scratch for every 64-value block, causing quadratic behavior for large segments. This was fixed in commit 810208889 (after the segmentation commit).

 ### 5. Linear segment scan (TODO)

 genericFindSegment does a linear walk through the segment list:

 │ "try binary search (might only make a difference for a very large number of segments)"

 For tables with many small segments, this adds O(N) overhead per lookup. The TODO was left to switch to binary search if profiling showed it mattered.

 ### 6. getSegments() is a workaround (TODO)

 getSegments() builds a new std::vector<const ColumnChunkData*> by collecting raw pointers from the internal std::vector<unique_ptr> each time, just to satisfy storage_info queries. The TODO suggests providing a proper std::span<const ColumnChunkData> instead.

 ### 7. Const-correctness workaround for ALP (TODO)

 rangeSegments has a const overload that does const_cast because ALP exception chunks modify state during scanning. The TODO notes this should be fixed.

records.title: Graphs (cpp/3310-remove-methods-from-project)
records.body:
**Languages:** cpp

# Graphs

## Video Solution

For more details about **Remove Methods From Project**, watch the walkthrough at [resources](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P7Txr3Y4GSQ).

## Concept

A directed graph models method invocations: an edge `a → b` means method `a` calls method `b`.  
Starting from the buggy method `k`, we can follow outgoing edges to find every method that is reachable—these are the *suspicious* methods.  
The removal rule states that we may delete the whole suspicious set **only if** no method outside the set has an edge pointing into it. In graph terms, we need to check whether there exists any incoming edge from a non‑suspicious node to a suspicious node. If such an edge exists, removal is impossible and we return all methods; otherwise we return the non‑suspicious nodes.

## When to Use It

Use graph traversal (DFS/BFS) when the problem describes:

- Relationships defined as “A invokes/calls/triggers B”.
- Need to find all nodes reachable from a source.
- Need to verify whether any edge crosses a boundary (outside → inside).
- Constraints up to 10⁵ nodes and 2·10⁵ edges → O(N+E) solutions are required.

## Template

```python
# adjacency list for a directed graph
graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for u, v in edges:
    graph[u].append(v)

# iterative DFS (or BFS) to mark reachable nodes from start
def reachable_from(start):
    visited = [False] * n
    stack = [start]
    visited[start] = True
    while stack:
        u = stack.pop()
        for v in graph[u]:
            if not visited[v]:
                visited[v] = True
                stack.append(v)
    return visited
```

---

## LeetCode Problem Walkthrough

### Problem: 3310. Remove Methods From Project

https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-methods-from-project/

### Approach 1: Brute Force (Repeated DFS)

**Algorithm**
1. For each method `i` (0 … n‑1) run a DFS/BFS from `k` to see if `i` is reachable.  
   - This yields the suspicious set but repeats the traversal for every node.  
2. After we know which nodes are suspicious, scan all edges: if an edge `a → b` has `a` non‑suspicious and `b` suspicious, abort and return all methods.  
3. Otherwise, return the list of non‑suspicious methods.

**Implementation**

```python
class Solution:
    def remainingMethods(self, n: int, k: int, invocations: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        # build graph
        g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for a, b in invocations:
            g[a].append(b)

        # helper: iterative DFS from k
        def dfs_marked():
            marked = [False] * n
            stack = [k]
            marked[k] = True
            while stack:
                u = stack.pop()
                for v in g[u]:
                    if not marked[v]:
                        marked[v] = True
                        stack.append(v)
            return marked

        # brute force: recompute the mark for every node (wasteful)
        suspicious = [False] * n
        for i in range(n):
            # we only need to know if i is reachable from k;
            # running a full DFS each time is O(N*(N+E))
            marked = dfs_marked()
            suspicious[i] = marked[i]

        # check for external incoming edge
        for a, b in invocations:
            if not suspicious[a] and suspicious[b]:
                return list(range(n))   # cannot remove anything

        return [i for i in range(n) if not suspicious[i]]
```

**Complexity Analysis**

- Time complexity: O(N·(N+E)) — we run a DFS from `k` for each of the `N` nodes.  
- Space complexity: O(N+E) — graph storage plus O(N) for the visited array per DFS (reused).

---

### Approach 2: Single Traversal + Edge Scan (Standard)

**Intuition**
The suspicious set is simply the set of nodes reachable from `k`. Computing it once with a single DFS/BFS gives us the answer in linear time. After we have the boolean `suspicious` array, we only need one pass over the edge list to detect any forbidden incoming edge.

**Algorithm**
1. Build adjacency list.  
2. Run one iterative DFS/BFS from `k` and mark all visited nodes as suspicious.  
3. Iterate over every invocation `[a, b]`: if `suspicious[a]` is `False` and `suspicious[b]` is `True`, an outside method calls a suspicious one → return all methods.  
4. If no such edge exists, collect and return all indices where `suspicious[i]` is `False`.

**Implementation**

```python
class Solution:
    def remainingMethods(self, n: int, k: int, invocations: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        # 1️⃣ build graph
        g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for a, b in invocations:
            g[a].append(b)

        # 2️⃣ mark reachable (suspicious) nodes from k
        suspicious = [False] * n
        stack = [k]
        suspicious[k] = True
        while stack:
            u = stack.pop()
            for v in g[u]:
                if not suspicious[v]:
                    suspicious[v] = True
                    stack.append(v)

        # 3️⃣ check for any edge from outsi
